threads_text: Sweden's Government Offices are blocking ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers from Monday and pointing everyone to Microsoft Copilot. The reason given is information security, since the other tools have no agreement in place. Would your workplace ever ban ChatGPT?
caption:
Sweden's Government Offices will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff work computers from Monday, Sveriges Radio reports.
Staff are told to use Microsoft Copilot, which was approved after a security review.
The Swedish Tax Agency already has a similar block.

Should governments let staff use any AI chatbot they want?

paragraphs.text: The Government Offices of Sweden, known as Regeringskansliet, will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff work computers, according to a report by Sveriges Radio's news program Ekot that SVT and Computer Sweden carried on October 23, 2026. The block takes effect on Monday, October 26, according to SVT and Mad Robot.
Staff are being directed to Microsoft Copilot instead. The Government Offices approved Copilot after reviewing it and raising its security level, SVT and Computer Sweden reported.

The Government Offices did not give a public explanation, according to Feber. Computer Sweden reported that Mikael Wettercrantz, the digitalization director, wrote on the internal intranet that using AI services without an agreement could have consequences for the organization's information security. The goal is to make sure employees only use services that have been approved.

The rule applies to staff computers rather than to AI in general. Feber and Mad Robot reported that the Government Offices has built its own AI assistant platform that still gives some employees access to Claude and ChatGPT. The press office did not say who has that access or how many people do, according to Mad Robot.
The Government Offices had already restricted the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek before this decision, Computer Sweden reported.
Other agencies and the Copilot question

The Swedish Tax Agency, Skatteverket, and the National Board of Institutional Care, known as SiS, have introduced similar blocks, and the Swedish Enforcement Authority, Kronofogden, is considering the question, according to SVT and Computer Sweden.

Mad Robot noted that Microsoft's documentation says Copilot can use Anthropic's Claude models, but those models fall outside Microsoft's EU Data Boundary and are switched off by default for organizations in the EU, EFTA and the UK. The Government Offices has not said whether Claude is enabled in its own Copilot setup.

The use of chatbots in government has drawn attention in Sweden before. In August 2025, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said he used ChatGPT and Mistral's Le Chat to get a second opinion, and his spokesperson said no security sensitive information was shared, Mad Robot reported. Ekot did not say whether the new block affects the prime minister's own use.
OpenAI and Anthropic had not publicly commented on the decision, according to Mad Robot.

The decision reflects a pattern in many large organizations. The question is less whether staff use AI and more which vendor has a signed agreement that covers where the data goes. Microsoft gains from that framing because Copilot sits inside software that government offices already license, while consumer chatbots used without a contract are treated as an information security risk, regardless of how capable they are.

The next step to watch is whether Kronofogden and other Swedish agencies adopt the same rule, and whether OpenAI or Anthropic sign agreements with Swedish authorities that would let their tools back onto official computers.
